To compress something means to reduce it — to make it take up less space, less time, or less volume than it normally would. Think of it as squeezing or pressing something into a smaller, denser form.

A simple image: hold a sponge in your hand and squeeze it. What was once a large, airy object becomes smaller and tighter as the air is forced out. You have compressed the sponge. That single image captures the heart of the word.
The three main ways "compress" is used

In its most literal sense, to compress is to physically press or squeeze something so it occupies less space. This applies to solids, liquids, and gases.

  • When you press down on a spring, you compress it. Its length decreases as its coils are pushed closer together.
  • Engineers compress gas into metal cylinders. What would fill a whole room of space gets packed into a small, heavy container.
  • A doctor might compress an injury — press down firmly on it — to stop bleeding. Here, the compression is steady, deliberate pressure applied to the body.
  • Cotton or wool is compressed into bales for transport. Loose, fluffy material is pressed into a tight, dense block that is easier to move.

An important nuance: physical compression does not destroy the material. A compressed spring is still a spring. Compressed gas is still the same gas. The substance is unchanged — only how tightly it is arranged in space has changed.

In the world of computers and technology, to compress means to reduce the size of a file, image, video, or other digital data using mathematical methods. The goal is to make the data take up less storage space or travel faster across a network.

  • When you compress a folder of files into a ZIP archive, you apply a process that encodes the data more efficiently. The same information now takes up far less space.
  • Videos are compressed so they can stream over the internet smoothly, without requiring enormous bandwidth.
  • Images on websites are compressed so pages load quickly. A photo that is 10 MB might be compressed to 1 MB while still looking acceptable on screen.

There are two important types of digital compression:

  • Lossless compression: the original data can be perfectly restored when you decompress (reverse the process). Nothing is lost — only the way the data is stored is made more efficient. ZIP files work this way. When you unzip, every byte of the original is intact.
  • Lossy compression: some data is permanently discarded to achieve a much smaller size. JPEG images and MP3 audio use this method. You may not notice the loss at ordinary viewing or listening levels, but the exact original cannot be fully recovered. The trade-off is: far smaller size in exchange for a small, usually acceptable loss of quality.
3. Abstract (figurative) compression — reducing time, length, or ideas

Compress is also used when talking about things that are not physical — like time, speech, writing, or complex ideas. Here, to compress means to pack more into a shorter span, or to express something in fewer words without losing what matters.

  • "We need to compress this two-hour presentation into forty-five minutes." — The same ideas must be delivered in less time, so some detail is trimmed and the rest is expressed more efficiently.
  • "She compressed a year's worth of learning into six months." — She worked intensely, covering a large amount of material in a short time.
  • "The editor asked him to compress the first three chapters into one." — Reduce the volume while keeping the essential content.
  • "He managed to compress his entire argument into one clear paragraph." — Express something complex in a dense, efficient form.

Here the "squeezing" is metaphorical — you are forcing a large amount of meaning or time into a small container. The pressure is effort and skill, not physical force.
What stays true across all uses

No matter the context — physical, digital, or figurative — three things are always true when you compress something:

  1. Something becomes smaller, shorter, or denser.
  2. Some kind of force, process, or effort is applied to achieve this.
  3. The essential substance or value is usually preserved, even if some detail is lost.

This last point is what separates compression from simply destroying or deleting. When you compress something, your intention is to keep the value while reducing the bulk.

Compress always works inward — reducing, condensing, packing down. Its natural opposite is expand (to make larger, more spread out) or decompress (to reverse the compression and restore something closer to its original state). When you decompress a ZIP file, the files return to their full size. When you release a compressed spring, it extends back out. Compression and decompression are a pair.

You can compress something a little or a great deal. Heavily compressed gas is under enormous pressure and holds a vast amount of matter in a small space. A heavily compressed piece of writing may feel very dense — difficult to read — because so much meaning is packed into so few words. The degree matters in practice: too little compression, and you haven't saved much; too much, and something important may be lost or damaged.
A range of sentences to anchor your understanding

• "Compress the gas into the chamber." — physics
  • "Compress the video file before uploading it." — computing
  • "Compress the report into a one-page summary." — writing
  • "We'll have to compress the schedule." — time management
  • "The nurse compressed the wound to stop the bleeding." — medicine
  • "He compressed decades of history into a single lecture." — figurative

In every case, notice the same pattern: something large, spread out, or long is being made smaller, tighter, or shorter — with the core value kept intact as much as possible.
